A.summary: Autonomy has inherent value; restriction is justified only when the exercise of autonomy fundamentally infringes upon autonomy itself.

B.summary: Autonomy is protected for party utility; restriction is justified if the utility gained by the parties exceeds the cost to the parties.

C.summary: Autonomy is protected for societal utility; restriction is evaluated by utility to society as a whole, with compensation required if party cost exceeds party utility.

c1.text: Autonomy should be protected because the value lies in autonomy itself rather than the consequences it brings.

c2.text: The originally intended will should be respected over what was expressed, even if the displayed intention differs and the other party relies on it.

c3.text: State intervention in autonomy is justified only when the exercise of autonomy so fundamentally infringes upon autonomy itself.

c4.text: Autonomy should be protected by focusing on the utility it brings to the parties, rather than the value of autonomy itself.

c5.text: A restriction on autonomy is justified if the absolute value of the cost (-) to the parties caused by restricting autonomy is less than the absolute value of the utility (+) gained by the parties.

c6.text: The mere fact that restriction of autonomy increases the utility of a third party (including the State or society) does not justify restricting autonomy.

c7.text: Autonomy should be protected by focusing on the utility it brings to society as a whole, rather than its value in itself.

c8.text: Restriction on autonomy is evaluated focusing on the utility to society as a whole rather than to the parties.

c9.text: If the absolute value of the cost (-) to the parties caused by restricting autonomy is greater than the absolute value of the utility (+) to the parties, restriction of autonomy is permissible only if the difference is compensated by the State, etc.

c10.text: To the extent of compensation by the State, etc., the utility of the parties is considered to have increased.

c11.text: When restricting the parties' autonomy, there are cases where the sum of the cost (-) and utility (+) to the parties is negative (-).

h1_1.text: One party unintentionally expresses intention ⓑ instead of the intended will ⓐ, and the other party recognizes ⓑ as the intention.

h1_2.text: The originally intended will ⓐ should be respected over the expressed intention ⓑ.

1.note: A holds that the originally intended will prevails over expressed and relied-upon intention, applying directly to ⓐ over ⓑ.

h2_1.text: When restricting the parties' autonomy is justified, the sum of the cost (-) and utility (+) to the parties is always positive (+).

h2_2.text: If the absolute value of a negative cost is less than the absolute value of a positive utility, their sum is positive (+).

2.note: Under B, restriction is justified only when party cost is strictly less than party utility in absolute value, so the sum is always positive.

3.note: Under C, whenever party cost exceeds utility, the State must compensate the difference; thus party net utility is always positive or zero. C cannot construct an argument for c11.

h4_1.text: The sum of the cost (-) and utility (+) to the parties caused by restricting autonomy is positive (+), but the exercise of autonomy does not fundamentally infringe upon autonomy itself.

h4_2.text: The parties' autonomy cannot be restricted.

h4_3.text: The sum of the cost (-) and utility (+) to the parties caused by restricting autonomy is positive (+), but the restriction generates a net cost to society as a whole.

h4_2.text: The parties' autonomy cannot be restricted.

4.note: Both A and C hold that autonomy cannot be restricted even if net party utility is positive: under A when autonomy itself is not fundamentally infringed, and under C when societal net utility is negative.

5.note: Country X's Act restricts autonomy based on net utility to society as a whole, which is supported by C (focusing on societal utility) but not by B (which explicitly rejects third-party utility as justification).

h5_1.text: The Basic Regulatory Act of Country X provides that the parties' autonomy may only be restricted if the total utility produced for society as a whole exceeds the costs generated by restricting autonomy.

h5_2.text: The restriction on autonomy under the Basic Regulatory Act of Country X is justified.
